en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Jewels, 87.
The Training Rule on Beds and Stools.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta was lying on a high bed.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings together with a number of bhikkhus, approached the dwelling of the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta.
The Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One come and see my bed.
Then the Blessed One turned back from that very spot and addressed the bhikkhus:
“By his disposition, monks, is a foolish man to be known.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son in many ways for being difficult to support...
[and so forth] ...and furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Furthermore, when a monk is having a new bed or bench made, it should be made with legs eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth, except for the lower crossbar; for one who exceeds this measurement, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.
“New” is said with reference to its being made for the first time.
A "bed" (mañca) means four kinds of beds:
one with legs shaped like elephant trunks, one with legs bound together like a bundle of sticks, one with legs shaped like crab claws, and one with detachable legs.
A "bench" (pīṭha) means...
There are four kinds of seats: one with legs shaped like elephant trunks, one with legs bound together like a bundle, one with legs shaped like crab claws, and one with detachable legs.
"By having [one] made" means either making it oneself or having it made by another.
It should be made with feet eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth, except for the lowest joint;

setting aside the lowest joint, if one makes it or causes it to be made exceeding that length, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of undertaking; upon acquisition, having cut it down, a confession of an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) must be made.
If one completes what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one has another complete what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation.
If one completes what was begun by others, there is an offense of expiation.
If she has it completed by others after it was begun by others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she makes it for another’s sake, or causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she uses it after obtaining what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one makes it the proper measure,
or makes it less than that.
If one obtains what has been made by another that exceeds the proper measure, and having cut it down, uses it;
except in the case of one who is insane or the first offender.
The fifth training rule concerning beds and chairs is finished.
